questions.stem: Which group of plants is called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' because they need water for reproduction but live on land?
questions.explanation: Bryophytes — mosses, liverworts, hornworts — live in moist terrestrial habitats but still need a film of water for their motile sperm to swim to eggs. This dependence on external water for fertilisation earns them the label 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'. Algae live fully in water. Gymnosperms (conifers) and angiosperms (flowering plants) evolved pollen tubes, freeing them from that water-dependency.

questions.stem: The largest group of plants in the plant kingdom is the:
questions.explanation: Angiosperms — flowering plants — include around 2,80,000 species, making them the largest plant group. They are divided into monocots (grasses, palms, lilies) and dicots (roses, mangoes, peas). Gymnosperms (conifers, cycads, ginkgoes) number only about 1,000. Pteridophytes (ferns) and bryophytes (mosses) are non-seed-bearing plants.

questions.stem: A plant with naked seeds (not enclosed in a fruit) is known as a:
questions.explanation: Greek 'gymnos' (naked) + 'sperma' (seed). Gymnosperm seeds sit exposed on cone scales, not enclosed in a fruit. Examples: pine, cedar, spruce, cycad, ginkgo. Angiosperms ('angeion' = vessel) enclose seeds inside a fruit. Ferns (pteridophytes) and mosses (bryophytes) do not produce seeds at all; they reproduce by spores.

questions.stem: The green pigment in plants responsible for photosynthesis is:
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue wavelengths of light; it reflects green, giving leaves their colour. Chlorophyll 'a' is the main pigment; 'b' is accessory. Carotenoids (carotene, xanthophyll) are orange-yellow accessory pigments responsible for autumn leaf colours and for the orange of carrots. Anthocyanins produce red, purple and blue in flowers.

questions.stem: The 'father of taxonomy', who devised the binomial (two-name) system of classifying species, was:
questions.explanation: Carl Linnaeus (1707-78), a Swedish botanist, introduced the two-name system (genus + species) in 'Systema Naturae' (1735) and 'Species Plantarum' (1753). Example: Homo sapiens, Panthera tigris. Darwin proposed evolution; Mendel worked on heredity; Haeckel popularised the term 'ecology' and coined 'phylum'. The hierarchy is K-P-C-O-F-G-S (Kingdom-Phylum-Class-Order-Family-Genus-Species).

questions.stem: The tallest living tree species in the world is the:
questions.explanation: The coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) of California reaches over 115 m — the record-holder is 'Hyperion' at 115.9 m. Not to be confused with the giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum), which is more massive in volume but shorter. Banyan (Ficus benghalensis) spreads widely due to prop roots but is far shorter. Teak and deodar are commercial timber species.

questions.stem: The study of fungi is called:
questions.explanation: Mycology — from Greek 'mykes' (mushroom). Fungi are a separate kingdom (not plants); they lack chlorophyll, have cell walls of chitin (not cellulose), and absorb rather than ingest their food. Yeasts, moulds and mushrooms are fungi. Virology — study of viruses; bacteriology — bacteria; entomology — insects; ornithology — birds; ichthyology — fish; herpetology — reptiles/amphibians.
